narrator.name: The Atlas narrator
narrator.voice: warm, unhurried, curious; a documentary voice that never oversells; speaks the dance's own words (names, counts) clearly
narrator.rule: The narrator only says what the profile says. Every sentence can be traced to a section, a claim or the music/movement DNA.
narrator.identity: one narrator for the whole atlas: the same face and animation everywhere; a native-speaker voice of the same character per language (studio-grade); the viewer chooses the language
narrator.wardrobe: in each episode the narrator wears the traditional apparel associated with the dance, reconstructed with meticulous care from the profile's costume notes and the licensed images — genuine and respectful, never a caricature; sacred, ceremonial or restricted attire is never worn (the narrator stays in neutral dress with a respectful nod in colour and fabric); the pack's visual_brief.wardrobe says which

scenes.title: Cold open
narration: The Lost Language of the French Court
This is Baroque dance. 17th and 18th century.
on_screen: Hero video, first 10 seconds (3uoHr22VmFQ)
Title card: Baroque dance · France · 17th and 18th century

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The style originated in the 17th-century French court under Louis XIV, evolving from Renaissance court dance.
It was heavily influenced by French, Italian, Spanish, and English forms, eventually becoming the 'belle danse' codified by masters like Beauchamp and Feuillet.
on_screen: Map: France · Europe
Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Originally performed at social events, court ceremonies, and theatrical productions like opera-ballets, it served as a display of elegance, social status, and artistic refinement.
Today it is a revived tradition.
on_screen: Footage: [ 09] Dance A Journey Across Europe, Choreographed By ' La Compagnie De L' Eventail' [ Etcohod] (https://archive.org/details/09-dance-a-journey-across-europe-choreographed-by-la-compagnie-de-l-eventail-etcohod)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance is characterized by an upright, refined posture and fluid, complex movements of the arms and legs.
It is highly codified, with specific steps linked to the musical meter of the period.
Watch for Five positions.
on_screen: Hero video full screen, 30–45 s (3uoHr22VmFQ)
Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Social ballroom patterns or theatrical stage paths.
scenes.music: diegetic (the video's own sound), underscore under narration

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Baroque dance is intrinsically linked to Baroque music, including suites, minuets, bourrées, and gavottes.
It is often accompanied by chamber music or court ensembles.
Listen for the Chamber ensemble, Court orchestra.
The pulse is Varies by dance type (e.g., minuet, bourrée)..
Characterized by the structured, rhythmic clarity of the Baroque period, often featuring strings and harpsichord, designed to support the precise footwork of the dancers.
on_screen: Instrument names on screen as each is mentioned
Listen later: Les Boréades — Jean-Philippe Rameau; Atys — Jean-Baptiste Lully; Les Boréades — Jean‐Philippe Rameau, Sabine Devieilhe, Reinoud Van Mechelen, Orfeo Orchestra, György Vashegyi (2024)

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Dancers traditionally wore elaborate, heavy costumes, often adorned with jewelry, reflecting the status of the nobility and the theatrical nature of court entertainments.
on_screen: Image gallery: 2 licensed images with attribution

scenes.title: The people
narration: Key figures include Louis XIV, Pierre Beauchamp, Raoul Auger Feuillet, Pierre Rameau, Melusine Wood, Belinda Quirey, Mary Skeaping, Wendy Hilton, Catherine Turocy, and Francine Lancelot.
Variants include the French noble style, English country dance, and less-studied Italian and Spanish court styles.
It is considered the first clear stylistic ancestor of classical ballet, with its technique influencing the development of later theatrical dance forms.

images.attribution: Henri de Gissey / Wikimedia Commons / Public domain
images.description: Louis XIV dans Le Ballet de la nuit. The ballet was choreographed in 1653. It was significant because Louis XIV made his debut at court. This court ballet lasted 12 hours, beginning at sundown and lasting until morning, and consisted of 45 dances. Louis XIV appeared in 5 of them. The most famous dance of Ballet de la Nuit portrays Louis XIV as Apollo the Sun King. Art by Henri de Gissey published
